articles.title: This 250-Lawyer Firm Had Exactly One Partner… And He Was Running A $700 Million Fraud
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

Which now-defunct Manhattan law firm, with roughly 250 lawyers and offices in five cities, wasn’t a partnership in the usual sense: it had a single equity partner, who was secretly running one of the great frauds in legal history behind it, peddling hundreds of millions of dollars in fake promissory notes to hedge funds?

Hint: In 2008, the firm founder was arrested in Toronto, for impersonating a pension-fund official in order to sell yet more phony notes, and his firm imploded within days.

See the answer on the next page.

articles.title: Legal Ethics Roundup: Supreme Court Recusals Derail Case, DOJ Targets Judges, Judicial Endorsement Controversy, Judge Leaks Sealed Records, Private Equity Rebuffed & More
articles.content:
Ed. note: Please welcome Renee Knake Jefferson back to the pages of Above the Law. Subscribe to her Substack, Legal Ethics Roundup, here.
#1 “Supreme Court Recusals Stop Music Case In Its Tracks, Strike Warning Note.” From NPR: “Something unusual happened at the Supreme Court this week: so many justices stepped aside from a case about music copyrights that the court could not hear it. … [Gabe] Roth and other experts said this is a good news, bad news situation. It’s a good thing the justices followed the recusal rules, they said. But the recusals in this case point to a deeper problem, said Renee Knake Jefferson, a legal ethics expert at the University of Houston. ‘When four justices need to step aside, the Supreme Court can no longer decide the case, and that becomes an institutional problem, not just an individual ethics issue,’ she said. This problem is acute at the nation’s highest court, because ‘there’s no other justices who can step in and substitute for them,’ Knake Jefferson added. Knake Jefferson said the justices who want to write books could put money from their advances and royalties in separate accounts, that they couldn’t touch until retirement. The court had no comment on that proposal.” Read more here.
#2 “Retired Judges Say DOJ’s Ethics Complaint Is Meritless.” From Law360: “A coalition of 61 retired federal judges has admonished the U.S. Department of Justice for filing a complaint against federal judges in Minnesota for speaking to a newspaper about the Trump administration.” Read more here.
#3 “NC Candidates Claim Chief Justice’s Support, but Judicial Code Bans Endorsements.” From The News & Observer: “As he serves his last full term, Paul Newby, chief justice of the North Carolina Supreme Court, has made his support for Republican judicial candidates clear. He’s headlined fundraisers, spoken at rallies and released a series of carefully crafted statements praising their qualifications. But there’s one word notably missing from Newby’s public support: ‘Endorse.’ North Carolina’s Code of Judicial Conduct bans sitting judges not up for reelection from officially endorsing any candidate — and Newby’s words of support have prompted formal ethics complaints, The News & Observer has learned. But that hasn’t stopped candidates from claiming Newby’s support in the election, posting quotes attributed to Newby on their social media accounts.” Read more here.
#4 “Judge Brown Emailed Sealed Court Papers to About 140 People.” From Bloomberg Law: “A federal judge under investigation for misconduct emailed confidential and sealed court papers to about 140 people in an early morning message, according to a new court order. A Judicial Council for the Fifth Circuit order Tuesday revealed the scope of US District Judge Ada Brown’s disclosure, which publicly confirmed the existence of a misconduct investigation into her conduct. The email also included sealed court papers in apparently unrelated lawyer disciplinary matters.” Read more here.
#5 “Why Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson Goes It Alone.” From CNN: “Now entering her fifth term on the Supreme Court, Jackson has taken an approach that in many ways has isolated her from her colleagues — stylistically and on the substance of the law. At the same time, she is reframing how the justices might look to the past to interpret the Constitution.” Read more here.
#6 “Who Gets to Know the Law?” From Kevin Lee in The Exile: “American law schools face a question that goes well beyond teaching students to use artificial intelligence. As machines become increasingly capable of producing legal research, drafting arguments, and analyzing complex bodies of doctrine, law schools must reconsider what lawyers need to know and what their education is supposed to accomplish. But there is another question that has received considerably less attention: How does the legal academy decide what counts as valuable legal knowledge in the first place?” Read more here.
#7 “TN High Court Says ‘No’ to PE Ownership of Law Firms but Other Options Open.” From Insurance Journal: “The Tennessee Supreme Court has rejected a rule change that would have allowed private equity companies to own law firms, blocking one avenue that insurance groups have warned could lead to more litigation, more high-dollar jury awards and higher defense costs. After reviewing comments from stakeholders, ‘the Court has not identified sufficient need or support for reforms related to non-lawyer ownership of law firms or fee-sharing with non-lawyers,’ the court wrote in its October order. ‘The Court may revisit this topic in the future as additional data regarding the success of these reforms becomes available.’” Read more here.
#8 “Court Rejects Attorney’s Assertion that Supervising eDiscovery Would Make Him a ‘Potential Witness.’” From JD Supra: “This case is a stark reminder that attorneys cannot outsource e-discovery obligations to their clients. Relying on unsupervised self-collection for electronic data may run afoul of Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(g), potentially exposing parties to ‘discovery on discovery’ and court-mandated supervised document searches.” Read more here.
#9 “‘Lawyer’ vs. ‘Attorney’: Is This A Thing?” From David Lat in Original Jurisdiction: “I combed through decades-old dictionaries and case law—and interviewed Bryan Garner, the longtime editor of Black’s Law Dictionary—to find out.” Read more here.
#10 “NC Legal Aid Groups Sue Over Lawmakers’ Redirection of Millions in Funding.” From North Carolina Health News: “Three North Carolina legal aid organizations are suing over lawmakers’ decision to redirect millions in IOLTA funding even as thousands in western North Carolina need services as they recover from Hurricane Helene.” Read more here (H/T Ellen Murphy).
This week you’ll find me in Austin, Atlanta, Detroit, and Washington DC, for a mix of meetings and celebrations. (I’m hoping Delta doesn’t let me down!) The highlight of my travels is on Saturday, when I will be at the U.S. Supreme Court to honor Judy Perry Martinez, a former president of the American Bar Association (ABA) who has been named the recipient of the 2026 Lewis F. Powell Jr. Award for Professionalism and Ethics. One of the highest honors bestowed by the American Inns of Court, the award recognizes individuals whose careers exemplify the highest standards of professionalism, ethics, civility, and excellence in the legal profession. I had the privilege of working with Judy as a reporter for the ABA Commission on the Future of Legal Services, which she chaired. She has since become a mentor and friend, and is so very deserving of this award.
Looking for other upcoming ethics events? You’ll find a list here.
Renee Knake Jefferson holds the endowed Doherty Chair in Legal Ethics and is a Professor of Law at the University of Houston. Check out more of her writing at the Legal Ethics Roundup. Find her on X (formerly Twitter) at @reneeknake or Bluesky at legalethics.bsky.social.
The post Legal Ethics Roundup: Supreme Court Recusals Derail Case, DOJ Targets Judges, Judicial Endorsement Controversy, Judge Leaks Sealed Records, Private Equity Rebuffed & More appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: Do It With Us, Not To Us
articles.content:
At a recent discussion, a leader described what he wanted from a technology provider: someone willing to work through implementation with his team.
He was concerned about the opposite experience. A large commitment. An expensive license. A provider eager to move ahead at a pace the customer could not absorb.
It was the kind of comment that makes you think about every obligation hiding behind the word “implementation.”
Clean the data. Find the process owner. Reconcile conflicting policies. Persuade people to use the system. Explain why the promised launch date has moved again.
Somewhere, a sales deck says “partnership.” On the customer’s calendar, that partnership can look like a second job.
Legal leaders should pay close attention to that gap. The success of a technology purchase depends heavily on how the parties work together after the contract is signed.
Ask The Vendor To Sit Through The Mess
A polished demonstration tells you something about a product. Watching the provider work through an actual customer problem tells you something about the relationship.
Take a contract review workflow. The official process may look straightforward: Procurement uploads the agreement, the tool flags issues, and legal reviews the exceptions.
Then someone explains that the supplier sent three versions. The business owner negotiated a concession by email. The playbook covers the U.S. entity, while the agreement names a subsidiary elsewhere.
Now the useful conversation can begin.
Ask the provider how it would handle that situation. Which information must the customer supply? What can the product resolve? Where does a person need to intervene? Which limitations will remain?
Pay attention to whether the provider asks thoughtful questions and can describe those limits clearly. You will need that candor when a real problem arrives.
Partnership Needs Names And Calendars
“Customer will provide reasonable cooperation” sounds harmless until everyone discovers how much cooperation the project requires.
Who is preparing the data? Who is configuring the workflow? Who can approve changes? How much time will legal, procurement, security, and IT need to contribute?
A credible implementation plan identifies those people and gives them work they can realistically perform.
This deserves attention during diligence. Ask reference customers what their teams actually had to do. Find out whether the provider’s implementation staff remained involved, how problems were escalated, and whether the promised support survived the sales handoff.
Head count alone tells you little about the attention your account will receive.
Legal can help make the workload visible before the business commits to a timeline that depends on several imaginary full-time employees.
Put The Promised Outcome Into The Working Plan
The debate about a SaaS reset has pushed value into the center of the buying conversation. Buyers asking harder questions about recurring fees should also examine what the provider needs to deliver the promised benefit.
If the goal is faster contract review, establish the baseline and define acceptable quality. If the goal is fewer escalations, determine which escalations should disappear and which remain essential.
Those distinctions matter. A falling escalation rate could reflect better decisions, poor issue detection, or users abandoning the workflow.
Value pricing makes the measurement choices particularly consequential. The parties need a shared understanding of the result, the evidence, and their respective contributions.
The statement of work should connect that understanding to delivery milestones, acceptance criteria, and a practical process for fixing problems. Otherwise, the value promise and the implementation obligations can drift into separate conversations.
Leave Room For The First Unpleasant Discovery
Every implementation has the potential to reveal something nobody understood at the beginning.
Perhaps the source data is unreliable. Perhaps a workflow depends on an undocumented exception. Perhaps users need a capability the original scope never addressed.
Agree on how the parties will handle those discoveries. Identify who can approve scope changes, how costs will be assessed, and what warrants pausing the rollout.
Starting with a bounded use case can help both sides learn before expanding their commitments.
Clear allocation of responsibility matters here. Shared accountability works when each party knows what it controls, what it owes, and where to seek a decision. A general promise to collaborate leaves too much room for an issue to circulate indefinitely.
Legal Can Make Partnership Concrete
Legal leaders can help the business translate an appealing sales promise into a workable relationship.
Bring the people doing the work into the evaluation. Examine their capacity. Connect the commercial model to measurable outcomes. Make sure the agreement provides a usable way to resolve the problems everyone hopes to avoid.
Then ask one final question before signing: When the first serious implementation problem appears, who will join the call with the authority and resources to solve it?
That answer will tell you quite a lot about the partnership you are buying.
Olga V. Mack is the CEO of TermScout, where she builds legal systems that make contracts faster to understand, easier to operate, and more trustworthy in real business conditions. Her work focuses on how legal rules allocate power, manage risk, and shape decisions under uncertainty. A serial CEO and former General Counsel, Olga previously led a legal technology company through acquisition by LexisNexis. She teaches at Berkeley Law and is a Fellow at CodeX, the Stanford Center for Legal Informatics. She has authored several books on legal innovation and technology, delivered six TEDx talks, and her insights regularly appear in Forbes, Bloomberg Law, VentureBeat, TechCrunch, and Above the Law. Her work treats law as essential infrastructure, designed for how organizations actually operate.
The post Do It With Us, Not To Us appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: The Elections: Grab Your Popcorn, And Stay Near Your Fallout Shelter
articles.content:
The elections in Israel will be held tomorrow, October 27.
Election Day in the United States is a week from tomorrow, November 3.
Grab your popcorn, and stay near your fallout shelter.
In Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu urgently needs the electoral support that an active war would garner for him. Bibi apparently tried to talk Trump into restarting the war in Iran, but Trump wants to delay until after the midterms.
Hmmm. Well, any port in a storm: There was a skirmish in the West Bank last week, and Netanyahu intends to use that as an excuse to light things up. He’s in the process of locking down the entire West Bank and demolishing local buildings.
What did I say: Any war in a storm?
The Iranians, of course, would love to screw around with the Israeli elections. Who knows what they might have planned for election day? Perhaps a relatively small attack on Israel by Iran or its proxies would make Israelis lose confidence in Netanyahu’s recent security achievements? Perhaps some well-coordinated cyber attacks could make transportation impossible on election day? Who knows?
Election Day in America follows one week later. Trump may decide that he needs a war in the next week, too. So far, his advisors have talked him out of starting the Iranian bombing runs in October, but as the polls grow worse, Trump’s need to do something — anything! — to change the discussion may yet prevail. If Trump doesn’t restart the war before November 3, he’s basically promised that he’ll restart it shortly thereafter.
The Iranians, of course, would love to monkey with the American elections just as fiercely as they’d love to disrupt the Israeli ones. I don’t know what Iran might have planned for next weekend, but my advice stands: Grab your popcorn, and stay near your fallout shelter.
Of course, that’s only on the international front. Domestically, things are likely to take longer to play out, but they’re sure to be just as weird.
Trump instructed the Department of Justice to file a lawsuit to prevent certification of the election results in the Alaska Senate race if the Republican loses in a close contest. The DOJ is now concerned that voters will be confused because two guys named “Dan Sullivan” are on the ballot.
Look: File as many lawsuits as you like to challenge ballot access before an election is held (and in state court). Make sure the electorate is choosing from among permissible choices. But don’t hold off on filing ballot-access lawsuits until after an election as a hedge against a result that disappoints you. Once the election has been held, don’t retroactively challenge the names of the candidates.
Can you challenge miscounting? Sure. Fraud? Sure. Other errors in the electoral process? Sure.
But if you want to challenge the names of the people on the ballot, do that before the election is held, so that those issues are resolved at the appropriate time.
That takes us up to a week from Tuesday.
After the elections, Trump will have lost at least one house of Congress, and he’ll feel unrestrained in his new lame duck status.
An unrestrained Donald Trump?
Grab your popcorn …
Mark Herrmann spent 17 years as a partner at a leading international law firm and later oversaw litigation, compliance and employment matters at a large international company. He is the author of The Curmudgeon’s Guide to Practicing Law and Drug and Device Product Liability Litigation Strategy (affiliate links). You can reach him by email at inhouse@abovethelaw.com.
